A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ProtocolBench, ProtocolRouter, and ProtocolRouterBench. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched across reformatting and renumbering.

before.justification: V1 reports original protocol comparisons across four scenarios, router-selection results, and router execution measurements in Tables 3–5.

after.justification: V3 retains these empirical results and adds worker-scaling measurements, a routing microbenchmark, and cross-model Streaming Queue results.

M1.justification: The router's constraint filtering, deterministic tie-breaking, optional priors, and stateless bridging remain unchanged in v1 Appendix F.9 and v3 Appendix H.9. However, v3 Section 3.2 describes native protocol wrappers replacing normalized retry/reconnect behavior, while Appendix F.1.1 still specifies disabled native retries and uniform PAL recovery. This conflict prevents determining whether the benchmark's communication procedure actually changed.

E1.justification: Both versions use GAIA, MS MARCO, 2WikiMultiHopQA, ChatDoctor-HealthCareMagic, and the same 60 router-selection scenarios containing 180 modules. The added model, worker-count, and overhead experiments vary configurations or isolate existing communication operations without establishing new dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: The evaluated protocol set remains A2A, ACP, ANP, and Agora. Router comparisons retain spec-only versus spec+perf and the corresponding best single-protocol baselines; the additional experiments introduce no new comparator.

E3.justification: V3 adds adapter-only measurements with 4–32 workers, a 1,000-sample localhost mock-executor routing test, and GPT-4o/Gemini-2.5-flash configurations. Section 3.2 also reports preserving native retry/reconnect behavior instead of v1's normalization, although Appendix F.1.1 contradicts this. Section 5.1 replaces stated P95/P99 summaries with minimum/maximum summaries. These are substantive reported evaluation changes, without establishing that retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: V3 adds analyses of adapter scaling with worker count, cumulative bridge costs, and sensitivity to the underlying LLM (Section 5.3 and Appendix F.6). These investigate overhead bottlenecks and generality beyond v1's evidence. The existing ablation list is retained, and the GAIA case study is relocated rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: V1 already describes bootstrap intervals and multiple-comparison correction. V3 supplies numerical Streaming Queue confidence intervals and adds Welch tests with Cohen's d and Holm–Bonferroni correction (Tables 4 and 10). The explicit three-run GAIA statement disappears; the PDFs do not establish increased independent replication.

E6.justification: Core scores remain unchanged: v1 Tables 3–5 correspond to v3 Tables 3, 6, and 7. V3 adds scaling results, a 0.80 ms mean routing-path latency, cross-model measurements, and the finding that ACP and A2A have no significant mean-latency difference. Table 11's end-to-end latency labels conflict with the retained seconds-scale results, so its entries cannot establish comparable-setting speedups. Appendix F.4 also newly describes the retained 6.5% relative GAIA gain as 6.5 percentage points.

T1.justification: V3 Section 5.3 introduces a heterogeneous-path latency decomposition and an additive bridge-cost argument: O(B) for fixed message size and O(BM), or O(HM), when size and hops are included. V1 has no corresponding analysis. This is a limited mathematical addition without a formal theorem or proof.

C1.justification: V3 recasts the advertised learnable/dynamic router as a constraint-aware, offline or low-frequency planner. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion emphasize constrained selection and metric-specific trade-offs, replacing broader superiority and security-preservation claims. The benchmark/router contributions and headline numerical gains remain.

C2.justification: V3 adds extensive mechanism explanations in Appendix D and expands limitations concerning model dependence, scale, cold starts, and changing workloads. It explicitly treats Fail-Storm discovery as a communication-continuity proxy, qualifies security findings by deployment configuration, and explains that bridging cannot automatically preserve a stronger upstream security guarantee.

D1.justification: V3 Appendix F newly lists exact releases: acp-sdk 1.0.3, a2a-sdk 0.3.3, agora-protocol 0.2.0, and agent-connect 0.3.5. These are newly disclosed versions, not demonstrated upgrades. V3 removes v1's explicit code/data repository link, while retaining artifact instructions and manifest placeholders.

R1.justification: The substantive related-work coverage and positioning against agent frameworks, benchmarks, and protocol surveys remain unchanged. The A2A source is reattributed from Google Cloud to the announcement's named authors, and other bibliographic details are updated without introducing a substantive new research comparison.

P1.justification: V3 substantially rewrites system-design explanations, metrics, result interpretation, and limitations. It consolidates the router evaluation narrative, adds Practical Guidance and Scope, expands terminology and qualitative-analysis appendices, and removes the LLM-use statement and acknowledgments. This exceeds a light editorial revision.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from a single-column layout to a two-column conference format, with extensively resized and repositioned displays. V3 adds Tables 4, 5, 10, and 11 plus a protocol-version table, removes boxed takeaways, and moves Figure 4 from the main text to Appendix F.4. Existing diagrams and core result tables are largely retained.

improvement.justification: V3 improves claim calibration, statistical reporting, and implementation documentation while retaining the headline results. However, its new native-retry description conflicts with Appendix F.1.1, and Table 11 labels Qwen/ACP latency as 0.148 ms end-to-end despite the retained 9.66 s result under allegedly matched conditions. These unresolved inconsistencies affect what was measured and how the added evidence should be interpreted, preventing a reliable net quality judgment.
